about: The editor's ideas across newsroom.sgit.ai, sgit.ai and php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, with outside evidence for and against

ideas.idea: Agents are the insider threat that never scaled: a reasoning engine in a loop with tools, with skills no human or static code insider had, that does damage without needing to be malicious.

where.quote: Agents are the insider threat that never scaled.
It does not need to be malicious to do damage, and when it is, it does damage at machine speed.

external_evidence.quote: Not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised, and the architecture of containment and control must account for that.
as employee negligence remains the biggest driver of losses
external_evidence.note: Human insider data: negligence, not malice, dominates cost. Vendor-commissioned (DTEX/Ponemon), via trade press.

external_evidence.quote: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system.
external_evidence.note: Nadella's unit is the model; the site's unit is one agent in one deployment.

ideas.strength: Strong: the CEO of Microsoft now argues the same frame in his own words, and insider-risk data shows non-malicious harm dominates; 'never scaled' itself is a framing, not a measured fact.

ideas.idea: The model-as-insider argument is now mainstream: Satya Nadella's 10 October 2026 post says what this network has argued since 30 September, ending on the same irony read from the other end.

where.quote: The argument is now mainstream.
His: the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours: the more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it.

external_evidence.quote: In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.
His post on X drew responses from Microsoft AI’s Mustafa Suleyman and Elon Musk.
external_evidence.note: Independent confirmation that the post is Nadella's; TNW describes it as a post on X, the long form is on snscratchpad.com, which does not name its author on the page.

ideas.strength: Confirmed: the primary post is captured and every quoted principle is in it; the claim of priority (since 30 September) is the site's own dated record.

ideas.idea: Models do not separate code from data, so prompt injection may never be fully fixed, and the controls have to assume a document can turn the agent.

where.quote: Models do not separate code from data. Instructions and content arrive in one channel, which is why prompt injection may never be fully fixed.

external_evidence.quote: As there is no inherent distinction between ‘data’ and ‘instruction’, it’s very possible that prompt injection attacks may never be totally mitigated in the way that SQL injection attacks can be.
“Prompt injection, much like scams and social engineering on the web, is unlikely to ever be fully ‘solved,’” OpenAI wrote
external_evidence.note: OpenAI's own post returned 403; quoted via TechCrunch.

external_evidence.quote: we bypass 12 recent defenses (based on a diverse set of techniques) with attack success rate above 90% for most; importantly, the majority of defenses originally reported near-zero attack success rates.
CaMeL, a robust defense that creates a protective system layer around the LLM, securing it even when underlying models are susceptible to attacks.
external_evidence.note: Complicates 'never fixed': a design-level layer outside the model can give provable security for a subset of tasks, which is the site's own remedy (controls outside the model).

ideas.strength: Strong: a national cyber agency, the largest model vendor and an adaptive-attack study say the same; only by-design architectures outside the model claim provable protection.

ideas.idea: What an agent can reach (the grant, measured) is not what it is for (the mandate); the gap between them is the risk, and an agent inherits everything its role accumulated.

where.quote: Reach is what it can do, measured. Mandate is what you asked it to do. The gap is the difference, in both directions.
the interesting number is the gap between what a credential allows and what its holder was meant to do. Agents made that gap the whole problem.

external_evidence.quote: less than 5% of permissions granted are used by workload identities
our research found that less than 2% of permissions granted to super identities are used, and 40% of super admins are workload identities.
Just 2%
external_evidence.note: The 2024 report gives about 2% of granted permissions used (all identities); the talk's numbers are from the 2023 report and are still the vendor's latest on workload identities in this capture.

external_evidence.quote: ambitions for highly autonomous agents raise complex long-term questions regarding scalable access control, agent-centric identities, AI workload differentiation, and delegated authority.

ideas.strength: Strong on the facts under it: the vendor's own telemetry shows grants far exceed use; the framing of 'mandate' as a written artifact is the author's.

ideas.idea: A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include; typed as boundary, setting, expectation or nothing, only a boundary is a control, and a rule the model keeps is hope.

where.quote: Barriers are what stands in the way of each row of the gap, typed as a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing, and only a boundary is a control.
A rule the model keeps is an expectation: hope. A limit the agent cannot reach is a boundary. Only the second is a control.
His most important idea is our enforcer test.

external_evidence.quote: a. The reference validation mechanism must be tamper proof.
external_evidence.note: The 1970s principle Nadella cites: the reference monitor.
external_evidence.publisher: James P. Anderson / USAF ESD (NIST archive)

external_evidence.quote: It’s why the controls that govern what a model can access and what actions it can take must sit outside the model.
agents must satisfy no more than two of the following three properties within a session to avoid the highest impact consequences of prompt injection.
by enforcing security policies when tools are called
The company conceded that “agent mode” in ChatGPT Atlas “expands the security threat s
external_evidence.note: Vendors still invest heavily in model-side defenses (adversarial training); the outside world treats them as one layer, not as the control.

ideas.strength: Established security principle (reference monitor, 1972) now restated by Microsoft, Meta and DeepMind for agents; the four-way typing and the hope percentages are the author's own, measured on invented designs.

ideas.idea: An agent's own logs and account of itself are a self-report, not evidence; evidence needs a record a hook reads, a platform boundary, or an outside test.

where.quote: The research agrees. Models that exploited a reward hack admitted it in under 2% of cases.
Evidence has four sources. The agent's account, a record a hook reads, a platform boundary, an outside test.

external_evidence.quote: to exploit the reward hack on > 99% of the prompts, but almost never (< 2%) verbalizes the reward
external_evidence.note: Wording drift: the paper measures verbalisation in the chain of thought, in 5 of 6 synthetic environments, not 'admitting' in logs.

external_evidence.quote: We need to be able to reproduce how an outcome was achieved without relying on the model to attest to it.
These results suggest that CoT monitoring is a promising way of noticing undesired behaviors during training and eval
external_evidence.note: The same paper treats CoT monitoring as useful, just not sufficient.

ideas.strength: Well backed: Anthropic's own study and Nadella's principles agree; the site's '<2% admitted' should read 'verbalised in its reasoning, in most test environments'.

ideas.idea: A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so somebody is already carrying it; there is no deny button, only three doors (accept for an interval, fund, fix), and silence escalates to the holder's boss.

where.quote: Every risk your organisation has is already accepted. Somebody is carrying it, today, whether or not anybody signed for it.
There are three doors: accept it for a stated interval, fund the work that reduces it, or fix it. Silence is not a fourth door.

external_evidence.quote: understanding or explicitly accepting the organization-wide risks being incurred from such decisions.
external_evidence.note: NIST requires a named official to explicitly accept risk.

external_evidence.quote: These include: (i) risk acceptance; (ii) risk avoidance; (iii) risk mitigation; (iv) risk sharing; (v) risk transfer; or (vi) a combination of the above.
external_evidence.note: Complicates 'three doors': NIST names avoidance (stop the activity) and sharing or transfer (insurance, contracts) as distinct responses.

external_evidence.quote: organizations might accept the risk associated with unfiltered connection to an external communications provider for a limited time
external_evidence.note: Time-boxed acceptance is already in NIST guidance.

ideas.strength: Partly backed: explicit, named, time-limited acceptance is standard NIST practice; 'no deny button' and 'three doors' narrow the standard set, which also includes avoid and transfer.

ideas.idea: Accepted (an act by a named person on a date) is not acceptable (a threshold); the EU AI Act asks for residual risk to be judged acceptable and never defines the word.

where.quote: Accepted is not the same as acceptable. One is an act by a named person on a date. The other is a threshold.

external_evidence.quote: the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable.
external_evidence.publisher: European Commission AI Act Service Desk

external_evidence.quote: system and to explicitly accept the risk to agency operations
external_evidence.note: US federal practice joins the two: the authorising official both judges acceptability and accepts, by name.

ideas.strength: Quote checked in the Act; 'never defines' was not checked against Article 3 in this pass, so that half rests on the author.

ideas.idea: Give each agent a licence to operate (who authorised it, who holds it, the policy, the expiry) that the system suspends when the footprint leaves the mandate, not a quarterly review.

where.quote: for each agent: authority, licensee, instrument, valid until. Accepted risks that expire and must be accepted again.
A named owner and an expiry for the risk that is left.

external_evidence.quote: The authorization termination date is established by the authorizing official and indicates when the authorization expires.
external_evidence.note: Authority to operate with an expiry is the US federal model since at least 2010.

external_evidence.quote: Organizations may eliminate the authorization termination date if the system is operating under an ongoing authorization
external_evidence.note: Continuous monitoring replacing the fixed date is NIST's version of 'suspended by the system, not by a quarterly review'.

external_evidence.quote: An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.

ideas.strength: Strong precedent: NIST's authorisation to operate already carries a named official, an expiry and an ongoing variant; applying it per agent is the new part.

ideas.idea: Autonomy is earned, each level unlocked by evidence that the one below held.

where.quote: write down what it can reach and what stands in the way, and you can give it autonomy inside that.
And autonomy is earned the same way: each level unlocked by evidence that the one below held.
where.note: Stated in the talk (talk.json beat licence), not in the source article.

external_evidence.quote: We argue that an agent's level of autonomy can be treated as a deliberate design decision, separate from its capability and operational environment.
We then highlight a potential application of our framework towards AI autonomy certificates to govern agent behavior in single- and multi-agent systems.
external_evidence.note: Autonomy certificates are close to the licence-to-operate idea.

ideas.strength: Moderate: academic proposals for autonomy levels and certificates exist; no regulator or standard yet ties levels to evidence that the lower level held.

ideas.idea: The more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it and the more autonomy you can afford to give it: brakes are what let a car go fast.

where.quote: Brakes are what let a car go fast.
the more you constrain an agent, the more autonomy you can afford to give it.

external_evidence.quote: In our internal usage, we've found that sandboxing safely reduces permission prompts by 84%. By defining set boundaries within which Claude can work freely, they increase security and agency.
external_evidence.note: A vendor's measured case of the irony: a boundary removed 84% of human prompts.

external_evidence.quote: Think of it like an emergency brake.

A study of crashes involving taxicabs in Munich of which half had been equipped with anti-lock brakes noted that crash rate was substantially the same for both types of cab, and concluded this was due to drivers of ABS-equipped cabs taking more risks.
external_evidence.note: Risk compensation: better brakes can be spent on speed rather than safety. The argument needs the autonomy granted to stay inside a measured envelope.

external_evidence.quote: We demonstrate effectiveness of CaMeL by solving $77\%$ of tasks with provable security (compared to $84\%$ with an undefended system) in AgentDojo.
external_evidence.note: Constraint has a measured utility cost.

ideas.strength: Plausible and echoed by Anthropic's sandboxing result and Nadella; the car metaphor has no traced origin, and risk-compensation research warns brakes can buy recklessness as well as speed.

ideas.idea: Footprint (what the agent actually did, read afterwards from logs) set against the mandate shows near misses and dormant rows, and for an agent with no written policy it is the fastest honest way to write one.

where.quote: Footprint in the gap is a near miss.
For an agent that has no written policy, it is the fastest honest way to write one

to create End User Accounts assigned to business functions rather than to human beings for the purpose of sharing files within or outside of the domain;
